title: Negation without Confusion: Decomposing Bias and Recomposing Style in Text Embeddings for Negation-aware Image Generation

paper.title: Negation without Confusion: Decomposing Bias and Recomposing Style in Text Embeddings for Negation-aware Image Generation
paper.abstract: Abstract Negation-aware image generation remains challenging for text-to-image diffusion models, which often struggle with negation due to implicit linguistic biases that are deeply entangled within text representations. As a result, bias-aligned semantics frequently dominate over intended negative constraints. To overcome this limitation, we propose a simple training-free method of De compose and R ec O mpose text embedding (DeRO), which constructs a semantic-preserving subspace and a bias subspace using auxiliary prompts and performs semantic disentanglement based on bidirectional SVD. By decomposing entangled representations and selectively recomposing disentangled semantic components, DeRO realigns text representations toward intended negation semantics while restoring residual stylistic features to preserve semantic fidelity and image quality. As a model-agnostic inference-time framework operating solely on text representations, DeRO can be seamlessly applied to diverse diffusion architectures, including both U-Net and DiT based models. Extensive experiments on both object- and concept-level negation demonstrate consistent improvements in negation-aware image generation, achieving stronger text-image alignment, better semantic fidelity, and higher human preference scores.

sections.heading: 1 Introduction
sections.text: Recent Diffusion Transformer (DiT) based text-to-image (T2I) models have achieved remarkable progress in visual quality and semantic alignment capabilities ( Labs, 2024 ; Podell et al., 2024 ) , but they still struggle to reliably handle negation prompts Li et al. (2024) ; Chen et al. (2025) . For example, even for a prompt of “a bakery without bread,” the undesired concept “bread” is often still generated as shown in Fig. 2 . A negation prompt inherently contains two coupled semantic components: contextual semantics to be preserved and target attributes to be removed . The difficulty of negation largely depends on the semantic bias between these components. When weakly correlated (e.g., room and bread ), the negated concept is reliably removed; however, strongly coupled pairs, such as bakery and bread , often persist in generated images. This mainly arises from implicit linguistic biases formed during large-scale training Geirhos et al. (2020) ; Park and Cho (2026) , which strongly entangle certain semantics within text representations Fu et al. (2025) ; Friedrich et al. (2023) . Therefore, negation in T2I models is fundamentally a problem of disentangling preserved and removed semantics rather than simply suppressing target concepts. Existing negation-aware generation methods mainly focus on suppressing unwanted semantics through attention manipulation Chen et al. (2025) or direct embedding suppression Li et al. (2024) . However, as illustrated in Fig. 1 (a), suppression-only methods struggle under strong semantic coupling Saha et al. (2025) , consequently suffering from semantic collapse, style distortion, or incomplete negation. To address these limitations, we propose DeRO ( De compose and R ec O mpose text embedding), a simple yet effective method that treats negation failure as representation-level bias entanglement. Unlike suppression based methods Li et al. (2024) ; Biswas et al. (2025) , DeRO constructs biased and semantic auxiliary prompt sets ( A B A_{B} and A S A_{S} ) and performs SVD based bidirectional disentanglement. Given “a bakery without bread,” the method selectively removes only bread-related semantics entangled within the bakery representation. Through semantic recomposition and residual style restoration before denoising, DeRO suppresses undesired semantics while preserving contextual structure and visual style. This representation-level intervention is supported by theoretical analysis, and fundamentally differs from methods relying on attention manipulation Chen et al. (2025) ; Biswas et al. (2025) or iterative sampling optimization Na et al. (2025) . Because the proposed method requires only a one-time auxiliary prompt construction stage and operates on low-dimensional embedding subspaces, DeRO introduces negligible additional computational overhead during inference. Furthermore, representation-level semantic decomposition naturally generalizes from object-level negation to more abstract concept-level negation scenarios. Without requiring parameter updates or additional fine-tuning, DeRO is model-agnostic and can be seamlessly integrated into diverse diffusion architectures, as demonstrated in both U-Net Rombach et al. (2022) and DiT based models Labs (2024) ; Podell et al. (2024) . The main contributions of this paper are as follows: • A simple yet effective training-free negation-aware generation method is proposed from the perspective of representation-level semantic disentanglement, which is model-agnostic and applicable to diverse diffusion architectures, including both U-Net and DiT based models. • An auxiliary prompt-driven bidirectional SVD strategy is introduced to disentangle bias-related semantics from text representations, while preserving visual style through semantic recomposition and residual restoration, supported by formal theoretical analysis. • Extensive experiments on object- and concept-level negation benchmarks demonstrate consistent improvements over existing baselines, achieving up to 27.4% improvement in TIFA score and 2.7% gain in PickScore, while consistently improving negation understanding in both conventional U-Net and recent DiT based diffusion architectures.

sections.heading: Text-Image Alignment.
sections.text: T2I research has primarily focused on improving text-image alignment through techniques such as reward optimization Na et al. (2025) , representation editing Arad et al. (2024) , and attention strength modulation Park et al. (2026) . While recent approaches such as DATE Na et al. (2025) and SoftREPA Lee et al. (2025) further improve alignment, they primarily target general text-image correspondence rather than the representation-level semantic entanglement inherent in negation prompts. More recently, negation-specific methods have emerged. SupEOT Li et al. (2024) performs explicit object suppression through U-Net-based interventions, while NAG Chen et al. (2025) employs attention extrapolation in transformer-based architectures. However, these methods rely on architecture-specific mechanisms, limiting their applicability in heterogeneous diffusion backbones.

sections.heading: Semantic Erasure.
sections.text: Concept erasure in diffusion models typically involves model editing Lu et al. (2024) ; Gandikota et al. (2023) ; Biswas et al. (2025) or text editing Li et al. (2024) ; Han et al. (2025) . While model editing often irreversibly alters model parameters and may affect generalization, text editing primarily performs global concept suppression but struggles with conditional negation, which requires context-aware selective removal. Although recent methods attempt to mitigate unintended side effects by localizing the erasure, such as leveraging graph-based spaces Bui et al. (2025) or null-space editing Li et al. (2026) , they still fundamentally rely on direct suppression of semantic directions.

sections.heading: 3.1 Motivation
sections.text: Recent diffusion models Podell et al. (2024) ; Labs (2024) have substantially improved text understanding and text-image alignment capabilities. Furthermore, recent architectures increasingly leverage multiple text encoders, such as CLIP Radford et al. (2021) and T5 Raffel et al. (2020) , to jointly capture global semantic context and fine-grained textual details. Despite these improvements, negation prompts remain challenging because removing a target concept requires suppressing not only explicit textual information but also implicit semantic priors learned from large-scale training data. Fig. 2 (a) illustrates this phenomenon using the prompt “a bakery with no bread.” Although the prompt explicitly specifies the absence of bread, the generated image still contains bread-related content. This failure suggests that the concept of a bakery is strongly associated with bread through implicit data bias, causing bias-aligned semantics to dominate over the intended negation constraint Kang et al. (2025) ; Orgad et al. (2023) . In contrast, as shown in Fig. 2 (b), prompts with weaker semantic associations naturally preserve the desired semantics while successfully removing the target concept. A straightforward solution is to project text embeddings into a semantic-preserving subspace using SVD based disentanglement. However, as shown in Fig. 2 (c), uni-directional projection often removes not only bias-related representations but also contextual semantics and visual style information. While the undesirable concept is partially suppressed, important characteristics such as scene identity and visual appearance can also be lost. To address this limitation, we propose a bidirectional SVD formulation that explicitly separates bias-aligned semantics from semantic-preserving representations while additionally restoring residual stylistic information. As shown in Fig. 2 (d), the proposed formulation removes implicit bias while preserving both semantic consistency and visual style, leading to faithful negation-aware generation. sections.heading: Problem Setup.
sections.text: Fig. 3 illustrates the overall pipeline. A key challenge in negation-aware generation is that negated semantics cannot be represented as an independent embedding, since target semantics are strongly entangled with contextual and stylistic semantics within pretrained text representations. For example, in “bakery with no bread,” bread-related semantics remain deeply coupled with bakery-related contextual semantics due to pretrained co-occurrence priors (more details are in Appendix B ). Consequently, direct suppression often removes useful contextual information or leaves residual target semantics in generated images. To address this issue, given a negation prompt p n p_{n} , two auxiliary prompt sets are constructed to estimate disentangled semantic structures. The semantic auxiliary prompt set A S A_{S} captures information that should be preserved under negation constraints, whereas the biased auxiliary prompt set A B A_{B} models dominant semantics aligned with the negated target attribute. Each prompt set is transformed into an embedding matrix, from which a semantic-preserving subspace 𝒮 \mathcal{S} and a bias subspace ℬ \mathcal{B} are estimated via SVD. The original text embedding x n x_{n} , obtained from the negation prompt p n p_{n} , is then projected onto 𝒮 \mathcal{S} while suppressing bias-aligned components within ℬ \mathcal{B} . Residual reconstruction further restores contextual and stylistic information, and the recomposed embedding x ^ n \hat{x}_{n} is injected into a frozen diffusion model for negation-aware image generation. sections.heading: Auxiliary Prompt Construction.
sections.text: In object-level negation, it is difficult to explicitly define a semantic state where the target attribute is completely removed. For example, in ”a bakery with no bread”, bread-related semantics remain strongly entangled with the bakery representation, making direct construction of a bread-free embedding highly challenging (See § B.1 ). Moreover, semantically similar directions may still preserve residual bias even after partial suppression Yin et al. (2019) ; Huang et al. (2025) . Therefore, instead of relying solely on a single negation prompt, we construct auxiliary prompt sets to estimate stable bias-reduced semantic structures. Specifically, we construct a biased auxiliary prompt set A B = { a b i } i = 1 N A_{B}=\{a_{b}^{i}\}_{i=1}^{N} and a semantic auxiliary prompt set A S = { a s i } i = 1 N A_{S}=\{a_{s}^{i}\}_{i=1}^{N} to refine the representation of the negation prompt p n p_{n} . To guide this process, we define the biased prompt p b p_{b} and the semantic prompt p s p_{s} . While p b p_{b} captures the target attribute to be removed (e.g., bread) along with its deeply entangled bias components, p s p_{s} preserves the desired contextual meaning without the target (e.g., an empty bakery interior). To ensure diversity and stability, the auxiliary prompts are iteratively generated using an LLM (e.g., Qwen2.5-Instruct) conditioned on p b p_{b} and p s p_{s} , respectively. In each of the N N rounds, the LLM generates C C candidates, and the one maximizing semantic similarity to its corresponding target concept is selected. Detailed LLM instructions and specific examples of these prompts can be found in Appendix D.1 and Table 1 .

sections.heading: Bidirectional Projection.
sections.text: Decomposing text embeddings requires careful structural manipulation, as implicit biases and contextual features are tightly coupled. Consequently, a naive one-directional projection inevitably creates a significant trade-off between bias mitigation and contextual fidelity. To overcome this limitation, we propose a bidirectional projection mechanism that simultaneously enhances semantic alignment while suppressing residual bias components. Specifically, the original negation embedding x n x_{n} is first projected onto the semantic-preserving subspace 𝒮 \mathcal{S} to extract the desired semantic representation, and the residual bias component is subsequently removed to obtain the bias-reduced semantic representation: x ^ n sem = ( 𝕀 − 𝒫 ℬ ) ​ 𝒫 𝒮 ​ ( x n ) , \hat{x}_{n}^{\mathrm{sem}}=(\mathbb{I}-\mathcal{P}_{\mathcal{B}})\mathcal{P}_{\mathcal{S}}(x_{n}), (2) where 𝕀 \mathbb{I} denotes the identity operator, and 𝒫 𝒮 \mathcal{P}_{\mathcal{S}} and 𝒫 ℬ \mathcal{P}_{\mathcal{B}} represent the orthogonal projection operators onto 𝒮 \mathcal{S} and ℬ \mathcal{B} (see Appendix D.2 for details). However, excessive semantic alignment may inadvertently remove stylistic information. To compensate for this effect, we utilize the residual representation after removing the bias component from the original embedding and project it onto the semantic-preserving subspace to restore contextual and style-related information: x ^ n style = 𝒫 𝒮 ​ ( 𝕀 − 𝒫 ℬ ) ​ ( x n ) . \hat{x}_{n}^{\mathrm{style}}=\mathcal{P}_{\mathcal{S}}(\mathbb{I}-\mathcal{P}_{\mathcal{B}})(x_{n}). (3) Finally, the semantic-aligned representation and the restored residual representation are combined to construct the final negation-aware embedding: x ^ n = x ^ n sem + x ^ n style . \hat{x}_{n}=\hat{x}_{n}^{\mathrm{sem}}+\hat{x}_{n}^{\mathrm{style}}. (4) The recomposed negation-aware embedding x ^ n \hat{x}_{n} is then injected into the frozen diffusion model, enabling negation-aware image generation while preserving the original semantic structure and visual style.

sections.heading: 3.3 Theoretical Analysis
sections.text: In this section, we theoretically analyze the underlying mechanisms of Uni-directional SVD (Uni-SVD) and Bidirectional SVD (Bi-SVD), confirming how DeRO resolves the fundamental trade-off between bias suppression and style preservation. The detailed formal statement and proofs are provided in Appendix C . We assume that a text embedding x n x_{n} is decomposed into entangled semantic, bias, and stylistic components within a shared embedding space: x n = x n sem + x n bias + x n style x_{n}=x_{n}^{\mathrm{sem}}+x_{n}^{\mathrm{bias}}+x_{n}^{\mathrm{style}} . Theorem 1 (Uni-SVD: Style Degradation) . Uni-SVD mitigates bias semantics through the operator 𝒯 uni = 𝕀 − 𝒫 ℬ \mathcal{T}_{\mathrm{uni}}=\mathbb{I}-\mathcal{P}_{\mathcal{B}} . However, because stylistic and biased components are inherently entangled (i.e., the stylistic representation shares significant overlap with the bias subspace ℬ \mathcal{B} ), 𝒯 uni \mathcal{T}_{\mathrm{uni}} inadvertently diminishes these stylistic features alongside the target bias, yielding x ^ n style = 0 \hat{x}_{n}^{\mathrm{style}}=0 . Consequently, applying a one-directional projection often leads to a noticeable degradation in visual style when bias suppression is enforced. Theorem 2 (Bi-SVD: Style Recovery) . In contrast, the bidirectional operator 𝒯 bi = ( 𝕀 − 𝒫 ℬ ) ​ 𝒫 𝒮 + 𝒫 𝒮 ​ ( 𝕀 − 𝒫 ℬ ) \mathcal{T}_{\mathrm{bi}}=(\mathbb{I}-\mathcal{P}_{\mathcal{B}})\mathcal{P}_{\mathcal{S}}+\mathcal{P}_{\mathcal{S}}(\mathbb{I}-\mathcal{P}_{\mathcal{B}}) overcomes this limitation through cross-subspace projection. Specifically, by additionally constructing x ^ n style \hat{x}_{n}^{\mathrm{style}} via cross-subspace projection, Bi-SVD explicitly rescues the stylistic content that Uni-SVD destroys. sections.heading: 4.1 Object Negation
sections.text: DeRO is applied to diffusion backbones including the U-Net based Stable Diffusion v1.5 (SD v1.5) Rombach et al. (2022) and Transformer based Rectified Flow models such as Stable Diffusion v3 (SD v3) Esser et al. (2024) , SDXL Podell et al. (2024) , and FLUX.1 Labs (2024) . Performance is evaluated using TIFA Hu et al. (2023) , a VQA based metric for assessing text-image semantic alignment, together with FID and PickScore Kirstain et al. (2023) to evaluate visual quality and the effectiveness of style preservation. We construct an evaluation set of 480 prompts starting from sentences in the ImageNet validation set. Using Qwen2.5-Instruct, we transform the original sentences into object-negation prompts containing explicit negation expressions such as ’without’ and ’no.’ These prompts are used to evaluate whether each method can selectively exclude the negated object while preserving the remaining semantics of the prompt. Performance comparisons are conducted against representative baseline methods in different diffusion backbones, including the Stable Diffusion v1.5 base model and its variants DATE Na et al. (2025) and SupEOT Li et al. (2024) , the SD v3 base model and its variant SoftREPA Lee et al. (2025) , as well as SDXL and FLUX.1 with its variant NAG Chen et al. (2025) . The quantitative results are summarized in Table 2 . Blue values indicate improvements relative to the corresponding base model, while Red values represent performance degradation. Table 2 presents quantitative comparisons of object negation understanding and image quality. Existing suppression based methods such as SupEOT and NAG improve negation understanding over baseline models, but often struggle to maintain image quality consistently. In contrast, the proposed method effectively improves both negation alignment and generation quality across different diffusion backbones. Under the SD v1.5 setting, DeRO achieves the highest mean TIFA score of 0.595 while improving PickScore from 21.245 to 21.815 and reducing FID from 195.207 to 193.091. Similar trends are consistently observed in SD v3, SDXL, and FLUX.1, demonstrating that auxiliary prompts effectively enhance negation understanding while preserving visual quality. As shown in Fig. 4 , existing methods tend to follow explicit sentence expressions. In contrast, negative attributes are effectively removed, producing semantically cleaner results, such as an empty cat bowl without residual water and a burger without cheese.

sections.heading: 4.2 Concept Negation
sections.text: For concept negation, we compare training-based methods, including MACE Lu et al. (2024) built on Stable Diffusion v1.4 (SD v1.4), UCE Gandikota et al. (2024) , and Erasing Gandikota et al. (2023) , with training-free methods such as SPEED Li et al. (2026) and RECE Gong et al. (2024) . Experiments are conducted on the artist negation benchmark Gandikota et al. (2024) ; following CURE Biswas et al. (2025) , we select 10 representative artists with 20 prompts per artist, where concept negation targets artist-specific semantic characteristics rather than contextual object co-occurrences. sections.heading: Effect of Bi-SVD.
sections.text: Fig. 7 (a) compares Uni-SVD and Bi-SVD under varying numbers of auxiliary prompts. Both improve over the base model, indicating that semantic bias disentanglement is beneficial for negation-aware generation. However, Bi-SVD shows more stable semantic alignment and visual quality, reaching optimal performance with fewer auxiliary prompts, whereas Uni-SVD improves more slowly. This can be attributed to the bidirectional projection mechanism of Bi-SVD, which further removes residual biased semantic components after alignment to the semantic-preserving subspace (Eq. 2 ), while Uni-SVD relies on one-directional suppression that may insufficiently disentangle bias or remove useful semantic information. Similar trends are observed in PickScore. In SD v1.5, incomplete suppression in Uni-SVD occasionally preserves stylistic information, leading to relatively higher PickScore values, whereas excessive suppression in FLUX.1 sometimes degrades visual fidelity. In contrast, Bi-SVD maintains stable PickScore performance while improving semantic alignment. sections.heading: Effect of SVD Component.
sections.text: Fig. 7 (b) presents the performance differences under varying numbers of SVD components ( k k ). Larger values of k k initially show higher TIFA scores, suggesting stronger negation behavior by capturing additional semantic variations associated with the target concept. However, as the number of auxiliary prompts increases, larger k k values exhibit bigger performance fluctuations and gradual degradation. This can be attributed to additional noisy components being introduced into the semantic basis together with useful semantic information. In contrast, k = 1 k=1 consistently achieves more stable performance and the best overall results, as the first singular component mainly captures the dominant semantic direction while minimizing unnecessary noise. Similar trends are also observed in PickScore, where k = 1 k=1 maintains more stable visual quality and stylistic consistency. Additional quantitative results are provided in Appendix E.5 .

sections.heading: 5 Concluding Remarks
sections.text: In this paper, we have proposed a training-free negation-aware generation method that disentangles entangled text representations through a bidirectional SVD-based decomposition-recomposition process between semantic-preserving and bias-suppressing subspaces. The proposed method not only suppresses undesirable biased semantics but also actively guides the representation toward the desired semantic direction while preserving the original semantic context and visual style of the input prompt. However, the proposed method still has limitations. Since semantic subspaces are estimated using auxiliary prompts, performance remains sensitive to prompt quality. Extending the method to more complex linguistic phenomena, such as relational and logical reasoning, remains an important direction for future work.

sections.heading: Appendix A Preliminaries
sections.text: Our method is built upon text-conditioned diffusion models. In text-conditioned diffusion models, an input prompt is transformed into latent representations through a text encoder τ ϕ \tau_{\phi} , and the generation process is guided by these text representations as conditioning information.

sections.heading: U-Net Based.
sections.text: Earlier U-Net based diffusion models Ho et al. (2020) ; Rombach et al. (2022) mainly relied on a single text encoder for conditioning. Given an input prompt p p , the prompt is transformed into a text embedding representation x x , which is injected into cross-attention layers to guide image generation. Typically, CLIP Radford et al. (2021) is employed as the text encoder, allowing image features to selectively attend to semantic information from the text representation and enabling text-guided synthesis.

sections.heading: DiT Based.
sections.text: Recent transformer based diffusion models, including FLUX.1 Labs et al. (2025) , SD v3 Esser et al. (2024) , and SDXL Podell et al. (2024) , adopt multiple text encoders to simultaneously capture semantic information at different levels. Instead of relying on a single text representation, these models utilize complementary embeddings obtained from different encoders. Specifically, CLIP mainly captures global semantic and contextual information and produces a pooled representation p pool p_{\text{pool}} , which is used in feature modulation to scale and shift intermediate representations before attention operations. In parallel, T5 provides token-wise contextual representations p emb p_{\text{emb}} , preserving detailed prompt semantics and compositional information. The complete conditioning set 𝒞 = p pool , p emb \mathcal{C}={p_{\text{pool}},p_{\text{emb}}} is integrated into transformer blocks, where text and image features interact through independent query ( Q Q ), key ( K K ), and value ( V V ) transformations. Such stronger text conditioning mechanisms significantly improve prompt fidelity by enhancing semantic alignment between text and generated images. However, despite these stronger conditioning mechanisms, generated images frequently retain undesired concepts under explicit negation prompts. In this work, we address this limitation by performing text embedding disentanglement directly within the text representation space prior to diffusion sampling.

For example, under profession-oriented prompts such as “a dentist examining a patient,” diffusion models often generate male individuals with a high frequency. This indicates that the profession embedding 𝐱 dentist \mathbf{x}_{\mathrm{dentist}} implicitly contains gender-related semantic priors rather than representing only occupation-specific semantics. When the bias direction can be explicitly defined by a single reference vector (e.g., 𝐱 man \mathbf{x}_{\mathrm{man}} ), the entangled bias component within a target embedding can be isolated via vector projection: 𝐱 bias = 𝒫 𝐱 man ​ ( 𝐱 dentist ) \mathbf{x}^{\mathrm{bias}}=\mathcal{P}_{\mathbf{x}_{\mathrm{man}}}(\mathbf{x}_{\mathrm{dentist}}) (5) We assume that the raw profession embedding (e.g., 𝐱 dentist \mathbf{x}_{\mathrm{dentist}} ) is linearly composed of its core occupational attributes (such as visual style or attire, denoted as 𝐱 style \mathbf{x}_{\mathrm{style}} ) and the entangled demographic bias ( 𝐱 bias \mathbf{x}_{\mathrm{bias}} ). sections.heading: General Token.
sections.text: However, extending this approach to general object-level concepts is challenging because semantic bias cannot be represented by a single explicit direction such as x man x_{\mathrm{man}} or x woman x_{\mathrm{woman}} . In practice, semantic bias is distributed across multiple correlated patterns. For example, in the prompt “bakery with no bread,” bread-related semantics are entangled with associated concepts such as cakes, trays, and food structures. Therefore, instead of relying on a single semantic direction, we construct semantic subspaces using multiple auxiliary prompts. Shared semantic components are extracted from related prompt embeddings, enabling more stable estimation of semantic information for negation-aware embedding construction.

The method assumes that padding regions in text embeddings still contain meaningful semantic information, and that removing such components can improve negation performance. However, unlike U-Net architectures, recent DiT models exhibit relatively cleaner padding embeddings with minimal semantic information. As shown in Tab. 7 , U-Net models demonstrate relatively high similarity between text and padding embeddings, suggesting that padding regions retain meaningful semantic content. sections.heading: E.1 Experimental Setup
sections.text: All experiments were conducted on an NVIDIA A100 GPU. To ensure a fair comparison, the number of inference steps was kept identical to the default settings of each corresponding base model, and a consistent random seed was used across all methods. Furthermore, all models utilized in this study were used in strict compliance with their respective licenses.

sections.heading: E.2 Uni-SVD vs Bi-SVD
sections.text: Fig. 12 provides additional qualitative results supporting the analysis in § 4.3 regarding the effectiveness of Bi-SVD. U-Net based models such as SD v1.4 and SD v1.5 exhibit unstable removal of target negation semantics when Uni-SVD is applied. As discussed in prior work such as SupEOT, the generation process of diffusion models is influenced not only by text embeddings but also by multiple factors including padding tokens and other latent interactions. Consequently, controlling only a single semantic direction through Uni-SVD becomes insufficient for resolving such complex semantic entanglement in a stable manner. In contrast, under FLUX.1, Uni-SVD gradually estimates more meaningful semantic directions as the number of auxiliary prompts increases, resulting in improved semantic disentanglement performance. This behavior becomes particularly evident in FLUX.1 because, as reported in previous studies Dalva et al. (2024) , the embedding representations of FLUX.1 exhibit relatively disentangled properties compared to other diffusion models, leading to more clearly separated semantic structures. As a result, dominant semantic components can be estimated more reliably even through simple unidirectional semantic decomposition, allowing Uni-SVD to achieve a certain level of semantic manipulation performance. However, for another Transformer based architecture, SD v3, Uni-SVD still fails to reliably preserve negation behavior despite its stronger text understanding capability. This observation suggests that the effectiveness of Uni-SVD is not determined solely by the backbone architecture itself. Unless the underlying embedding representations already possess disentangled semantic structures similar to FLUX.1, Uni-SVD remains limited in handling strongly entangled semantic scenarios. In contrast, the proposed Bi-SVD forms a more robust semantic subspace as the number of auxiliary prompts increases, allowing semantic directions to be estimated more reliably while simultaneously separating semantic and stylistic information through bidirectional decomposition. These results suggest that simple unidirectional suppression strategies are difficult to generalize across diverse diffusion backbones, whereas the proposed bidirectional decomposition framework provides a more robust and generalizable solution for negation-aware generation.

sections.heading: E.3 Concept Negation
sections.text: Figure 13: Qualitative results of concept negation with varying numbers of auxiliary prompts. For concept-level negation, DeRO uses only a single auxiliary semantic prompt ( A S A_{S} ) and a single manually defined biased prompt ( A B A_{B} ) by default. Unlike object-level negation, where target semantics are often strongly entangled with surrounding contextual information, concept-level semantics are generally more directly associated with the target concept itself. As a result, the dependency on multiple auxiliary prompts becomes substantially lower, and stable semantic removal can already be achieved using a single auxiliary prompt pair across different diffusion backbones. Additional qualitative comparisons are provided in Fig. 13 .

sections.heading: E.4 Extraction Method
sections.text: Figure 14: Qualitative comparisons of different component decomposition methods under single and multi-negation settings. Concept negation evaluates whether concept-specific characteristics remain despite explicit negation prompts; for example, given a prompt p n p_{n} such as “a garden not in the style of Monet”, we assess whether Monet-style characteristics are successfully removed from generated images using artistic concepts. Fig. 14 provides additional qualitative results for the analysis in § 4.3 (Extraction Method). To investigate the effect of component extraction methods for semantic basis decomposition in the prompt embedding space, we compare Mean, Principal Component Analysis ( PCA ), Independent Component Analysis ( ICA ), Robust Principal Component Analysis ( RPCA ), and Singular Value Decomposition ( SVD ) under both single-negation and multi-negation settings. Mean exhibits the weakest performance because simple averaging fails to effectively suppress shared biased semantics, resulting in residual bias in generated images. RPCA exhibits the most unstable behavior. RPCA assumes that the input representation can be decomposed into low-rank structures and sparse residual components. However, auxiliary prompts often contain meaningful semantic variations rather than sparse noise. Consequently, some semantic information may be incorrectly separated into sparse residual components, distorting the underlying semantic structure of the embedding space and degrading both semantic consistency and image quality. As shown on the left side of Fig. 14 , this effect becomes more noticeable as the number of auxiliary prompts increases, leading to increasingly blurry generated results. While PCA and ICA are highly effective at capturing simple, dominant semantic structures, they fail to maintain semantic consistency in complex, multi-negation scenarios. In single-negation settings, PCA extracts dominant semantic directions through variance maximization, whereas ICA aims to separate statistically independent latent components; both methods perform reliably because the underlying semantic patterns are straightforward. However, in multi-negation scenarios, multiple semantic attributes become simultaneously entangled and interact with each other within the text representation. For instance, under complex prompts such as “ not filled with iced coffee ,” both methods struggle to consistently satisfy multiple semantic conditions. This demonstrates that relying solely on dominant directions or independent components is insufficient for representing intertwined semantic factors, ultimately leading to a degradation of semantic consistency. SVD consistently demonstrates the most robust behavior across different settings. Unlike PCA , which tends to be sensitive to dominant, high-variance semantic factors, SVD estimates the principal semantic structures repeatedly shared across auxiliary prompts in a much more stable manner. Given that multiple entangled semantic directions coexist in multi-negation scenarios, the stable estimation of these shared structures becomes increasingly critical. Consequently, SVD achieves more reliable semantic disentanglement and better preserves semantic consistency across diverse and complex conditions.

sections.heading: E.5 SVD Component
sections.text: Figure 15: Qualitative comparisons with different numbers of SVD components ( k k ). Fig. 15 provides additional qualitative results for the analysis in § 4.3 (Effect of SVD Component). The results show that using only k = 1 k=1 is sufficient to capture the dominant semantic direction shared across auxiliary prompts, enabling stable semantic disentanglement. In contrast, including additional components tends to introduce finer semantic variations, contextual information, and residual stylistic representations. Since these components are not always directly related to negation semantics, they may distort the original semantic structure or weaken negation performance. Therefore, we use only the first singular component in all experiments. Figure 16: Qualitative comparisons for nude concept negation across SD v1.4, SD v1.5, FLUX.1, and SDXL. Regions highlighted with red markers indicate failure cases in the base model, whereas regions highlighted with blue markers correspond to improvements achieved by DeRO.

sections.heading: F.1 Nude Concept Negation
sections.text: ** As this section involves sensitive visual concepts, the proposed framework is intended solely for research purposes to evaluate semantic disentanglement and negation understanding, rather than for generating or modifying inappropriate content. ** To evaluate the generalization capability of DeRO, we conduct additional nude concept negation experiments using a dataset adapted from Gong et al. (2024) across SD v1.4, SD v1.5, FLUX.1, and SDXL. Similar to artist concept negation, where strong semantic associations are induced by artist identities, nude concept negation also exhibits strong concept-specific priors embedded within pretrained text representations. Consequently, diffusion models often retain nudity-related semantics even under explicit negation prompts such as without nudity . To examine whether generated images correctly follow prompts containing explicit negation expressions, we apply DeRO and present qualitative results in Fig. 16 . Compared to the base models, DeRO demonstrates substantially improved adherence to the input prompts. Specifically, DeRO consistently suppresses nudity-related biased semantics while preserving clothing structure, human posture, and overall visual realism across different diffusion backbones. These results suggest that the proposed Bi-SVD based decomposition effectively generalizes beyond artist-style negation toward broader semantic concept negation scenarios.

sections.heading: F.2 Additional Application
sections.text: DeRO is additionally evaluated on FLUX.1-schnell Labs (2024) , a distilled version of FLUX.1. The results show that DeRO can also be effectively applied to distilled diffusion models. However, due to compressed semantic representations introduced by the distillation process, semantic subspace estimation becomes relatively unstable when only a limited number of auxiliary prompts are available. To compensate for this limitation, we use 12 auxiliary prompts in our experiments. Qualitative examples are in Fig. 22 .

sections.heading: Appendix H User Study Details
sections.text: We conduct a human evaluation of object- and concept-level negation using FLUX.1, which achieved the best overall performance in the main experiments. For object negation, we compare the FLUX.1 base model, NAG, and DeRO, while for concept negation, we compare the FLUX.1 base model, Erasing, and DeRO. A total of 32 volunteers participated without financial compensation. All participants provided informed consent prior to the study and were informed that their responses would be used solely for research purposes. The sample size was determined through a power analysis following Cohen Cohen (1960) , assuming a large effect size ( d = 0.8 d=0.8 ), power of 0.8 0.8 , and a significance level of α = 0.05 \alpha=0.05 . Each participant evaluated 12 randomly sampled prompts for each negation type and ranked the three generated images based on Prompt Alignment and Visual Quality , measuring adherence to the prompt including the specified negation and overall perceptual quality, respectively. The rankings were converted into Borda scores of 1.0 1.0 , 0.5 0.5 , and 0.0 0.0 for first, second, and third place, respectively, accumulated across all participants and prompts, and normalized by the maximum possible score. The resulting preference scores are reported in Tab. 4 . Wilcoxon signed-rank tests on participant-level responses show that DeRO significantly outperforms the competing methods across all four criteria: Object Alignment ( p = 3.6 × 10 − 7 p=3.6\times 10^{-7} ), Object Visual Quality ( p = 3.8 × 10 − 7 p=3.8\times 10^{-7} ), Concept Alignment ( p = 3.7 × 10 − 7 p=3.7\times 10^{-7} ), and Concept Visual Quality ( p = 3.8 × 10 − 7 p=3.8\times 10^{-7} ), with all differences significant at p < 0.001 p<0.001 . The evaluation instructions and example questions are provided in Fig. 17 .

As a result, bias-aligned semantics frequently dominate over intended negative constraints. To overcome this limitation, we propose a simple training-free method of De compose and R ec O mpose text embedding (DeRO), which constructs a semantic-preserving subspace and a bias subspace using auxiliary prompts and performs semantic disentanglement based on bidirectional SVD. By decomposing entangled representations and selectively recomposing disentangled semantic components, DeRO realigns text representations toward intended negation semantics while restoring residual stylistic features to preserve semantic fidelity and image quality. As a model-agnostic inference-time framework operating solely on text representations, DeRO can be seamlessly applied to diverse diffusion architectures, including both U-Net and DiT based models. Extensive experiments on both object- and concept-level negation demonstrate consistent improvements in negation-aware image generation, achieving stronger text-image alignment, better semantic fidelity, and higher human preference scores. Figure 1: (a) Existing unidirectional SVD methods (e.g., SupEOT Li et al. (2024) ) suppress only bias or negation directions within padding representations in order to remove undesired information while preserving the original prompt style. However, due to the strong entanglement among semantic, stylistic, and bias components, residual biased semantics often remain in the text embedding, resulting in incomplete negation or degraded stylistic consistency. (b) In contrast, bidirectional SVD operates in a universal embedding, enabling precise removal of bias components while preserving semantic and stylistic information, thereby achieving faithful negation-aware generation. 1 Introduction Recent Diffusion Transformer (DiT) based text-to-image (T2I) models have achieved remarkable progress in visual quality and semantic alignment capabilities ( Labs, 2024 ; Podell et al., 2024 ) , but they still struggle to reliably handle negation prompts Li et al. (2024) ; Chen et al. (2025) . For example, even for a prompt of “a bakery without bread,” the undesired concept “bread” is often still generated as shown in Fig. 2 . A negation prompt inherently contains two coupled semantic components: contextual semantics to be preserved and target attributes to be removed . The difficulty of negation largely depends on the semantic bias between these components. When weakly correlated (e.g., room and bread ), the negated concept is reliably removed; however, strongly coupled pairs, such as bakery and bread , often persist in generated images. This mainly arises from implicit linguistic biases formed during large-scale training Geirhos et al. (2020) ; Park and Cho (2026) , which strongly entangle certain semantics within text representations Fu et al. (2025) ; Friedrich et al. (2023) . Therefore, negation in T2I models is fundamentally a problem of disentangling preserved and removed semantics rather than simply suppressing target concepts. Existing negation-aware generation methods mainly focus on suppressing unwanted semantics through attention manipulation Chen et al. (2025) or direct embedding suppression Li et al. (2024) . However, as illustrated in Fig. 1 (a), suppression-only methods struggle under strong semantic coupling Saha et al. (2025) , consequently suffering from semantic collapse, style distortion, or incomplete negation. To address these limitations, we propose DeRO ( De compose and R ec O mpose text embedding), a simple yet effective method that treats negation failure as representation-level bias entanglement. Unlike suppression based methods Li et al. (2024) ; Biswas et al. (2025) , DeRO constructs biased and semantic auxiliary prompt sets ( A B A_{B} and A S A_{S} ) and performs SVD based bidirectional disentanglement. Given “a bakery without bread,” the method selectively removes only bread-related semantics entangled within the bakery representation. Through semantic recomposition and residual style restoration before denoising, DeRO suppresses undesired semantics while preserving contextual structure and visual style. This representation-level intervention is supported by theoretical analysis, and fundamentally differs from methods relying on attention manipulation Chen et al. (2025) ; Biswas et al. (2025) or iterative sampling optimization Na et al. (2025) . Because the proposed method requires only a one-time auxiliary prompt construction stage and operates on low-dimensional embedding subspaces, DeRO introduces negligible additional computational overhead during inference. Furthermore, representation-level semantic decomposition naturally generalizes from object-level negation to more abstract concept-level negation scenarios. Without requiring parameter updates or additional fine-tuning, DeRO is model-agnostic and can be seamlessly integrated into diverse diffusion architectures, as demonstrated in both U-Net Rombach et al. (2022) and DiT based models Labs (2024) ; Podell et al. (2024) . The main contributions of this paper are as follows: • A simple yet effective training-free negation-aware generation method is proposed from the perspective of representation-level semantic disentanglement, which is model-agnostic and applicable to diverse diffusion architectures, including both U-Net and DiT based models. • An auxiliary prompt-driven bidirectional SVD strategy is introduced to disentangle bias-related semantics from text representations, while preserving visual style through semantic recomposition and residual restoration, supported by formal theoretical analysis. • Extensive experiments on object- and concept-level negation benchmarks demonstrate consistent improvements over existing baselines, achieving up to 27.4% improvement in TIFA score and 2.7% gain in PickScore, while consistently improving negation understanding in both conventional U-Net and recent DiT based diffusion architectures. 2 Related Work Text-Image Alignment. T2I research has primarily focused on improving text-image alignment through techniques such as reward optimization Na et al. (2025) , representation editing Arad et al. (2024) , and attention strength modulation Park et al. (2026) . While recent approaches such as DATE Na et al. (2025) and SoftREPA Lee et al. (2025) further improve alignment, they primarily target general text-image correspondence rather than the representation-level semantic entanglement inherent in negation prompts. More recently, negation-specific methods have emerged. SupEOT Li et al. (2024) performs explicit object suppression through U-Net-based interventions, while NAG Chen et al. (2025) employs attention extrapolation in transformer-based architectures. However, these methods rely on architecture-specific mechanisms, limiting their applicability in heterogeneous diffusion backbones. Semantic Erasure. Concept erasure in diffusion models typically involves model editing Lu et al. (2024) ; Gandikota et al. (2023) ; Biswas et al. (2025) or text editing Li et al. (2024) ; Han et al. (2025) . While model editing often irreversibly alters model parameters and may affect generalization, text editing primarily performs global concept suppression but struggles with conditional negation, which requires context-aware selective removal. Although recent methods attempt to mitigate unintended side effects by localizing the erasure, such as leveraging graph-based spaces Bui et al. (2025) or null-space editing Li et al. (2026) , they still fundamentally rely on direct suppression of semantic directions. 3 Proposed Method 3.1 Motivation Recent diffusion models Podell et al. (2024) ; Labs (2024) have substantially improved text understanding and text-image alignment capabilities. Furthermore, recent architectures increasingly leverage multiple text encoders, such as CLIP Radford et al. (2021) and T5 Raffel et al. (2020) , to jointly capture global semantic context and fine-grained textual details. Despite these improvements, negation prompts remain challenging because removing a target concept requires suppressing not only explicit textual information but also implicit semantic priors learned from large-scale training data. Fig. 2 (a) illustrates this phenomenon using the prompt “a bakery with no bread.” Although the prompt explicitly specifies the absence of bread, the generated image still contains bread-related content. This failure suggests that the concept of a bakery is strongly associated with bread through implicit data bias, causing bias-aligned semantics to dominate over the intended negation constraint Kang et al. (2025) ; Orgad et al. (2023) . In contrast, as shown in Fig. 2 (b), prompts with weaker semantic associations naturally preserve the desired semantics while successfully removing the target concept. A straightforward solution is to project text embeddings into a semantic-preserving subspace using SVD based disentanglement. However, as shown in Fig. 2 (c), uni-directional projection often removes not only bias-related representations but also contextual semantics and visual style information. While the undesirable concept is partially suppressed, important characteristics such as scene identity and visual appearance can also be lost. To address this limitation, we propose a bidirectional SVD formulation that explicitly separates bias-aligned semantics from semantic-preserving representations while additionally restoring residual stylistic information. As shown in Fig. 2 (d), the proposed formulation removes implicit bias while preserving both semantic consistency and visual style, leading to faithful negation-aware generation. For each result, the left mark indicates whether the negation constraint is satisfied, and the right mark indicates whether the original contextual style (e.g., bakery interior) is preserved. Figure 3: Overview of DeRO. (Step 1) Biased and semantic auxiliary prompts are iteratively generated via an LLM and ranked by semantic similarity. (Step 2) Text embeddings of auxiliary prompts are encoded and decomposed via SVD to estimate the semantic basis V 𝒮 ( k ) V^{(k)}_{\mathcal{S}} and bias basis V ℬ ( k ) V^{(k)}_{\mathcal{B}} . (Step 3) Bidirectional projection constructs x ^ n = x ^ n sem + x ^ n style \hat{x}_{n}=\hat{x}_{n}^{\mathrm{sem}}+\hat{x}_{n}^{\mathrm{style}} via two directions. Direction 1 removes bias after semantic alignment, and Direction 2 restores style after bias removal. (Step 4) The recomposed negation-aware embedding x ^ n \hat{x}_{n} is applied for image generation. 3.2 Negation-aware Text Embedding Problem Setup. Fig. 3 illustrates the overall pipeline. A key challenge in negation-aware generation is that negated semantics cannot be represented as an independent embedding, since target semantics are strongly entangled with contextual and stylistic semantics within pretrained text representations. For example, in “bakery with no bread,” bread-related semantics remain deeply coupled with bakery-related contextual semantics due to pretrained co-occurrence priors (more details are in Appendix B ). Consequently, direct suppression often removes useful contextual information or leaves residual target semantics in generated images. To address this issue, given a negation prompt p n p_{n} , two auxiliary prompt sets are constructed to estimate disentangled semantic structures. The semantic auxiliary prompt set A S A_{S} captures information that should be preserved under negation constraints, whereas the biased auxiliary prompt set A B A_{B} models dominant semantics aligned with the negated target attribute. Each prompt set is transformed into an embedding matrix, from which a semantic-preserving subspace 𝒮 \mathcal{S} and a bias subspace ℬ \mathcal{B} are estimated via SVD. Auxiliary Prompt Construction. In object-level negation, it is difficult to explicitly define a semantic state where the target attribute is completely removed. For example, in ”a bakery with no bread”, bread-related semantics remain strongly entangled with the bakery representation, making direct construction of a bread-free embedding highly challenging (See § B.1 ). Moreover, semantically similar directions may still preserve residual bias even after partial suppression Yin et al. (2019) ; Huang et al. (2025) . Therefore, instead of relying solely on a single negation prompt, we construct auxiliary prompt sets to estimate stable bias-reduced semantic structures. Specifically, we construct a biased auxiliary prompt set A B = { a b i } i = 1 N A_{B}=\{a_{b}^{i}\}_{i=1}^{N} and a semantic auxiliary prompt set A S = { a s i } i = 1 N A_{S}=\{a_{s}^{i}\}_{i=1}^{N} to refine the representation of the negation prompt p n p_{n} . To guide this process, we define the biased prompt p b p_{b} and the semantic prompt p s p_{s} . While p b p_{b} captures the target attribute to be removed (e.g., bread) along with its deeply entangled bias components, p s p_{s} preserves the desired contextual meaning without the target (e.g., an empty bakery interior). To ensure diversity and stability, the auxiliary prompts are iteratively generated using an LLM (e.g., Qwen2.5-Instruct) conditioned on p b p_{b} and p s p_{s} , respectively. In each of the N N rounds, the LLM generates C C candidates, and the one maximizing semantic similarity to its corresponding target concept is selected. Decomposing text embeddings requires careful structural manipulation, as implicit biases and contextual features are tightly coupled. Consequently, a naive one-directional projection inevitably creates a significant trade-off between bias mitigation and contextual fidelity. To overcome this limitation, we propose a bidirectional projection mechanism that simultaneously enhances semantic alignment while suppressing residual bias components. Specifically, the original negation embedding x n x_{n} is first projected onto the semantic-preserving subspace 𝒮 \mathcal{S} to extract the desired semantic representation, and the residual bias component is subsequently removed to obtain the bias-reduced semantic representation: x ^ n sem = ( 𝕀 − 𝒫 ℬ ) ​ 𝒫 𝒮 ​ ( x n ) , \hat{x}_{n}^{\mathrm{sem}}=(\mathbb{I}-\mathcal{P}_{\mathcal{B}})\mathcal{P}_{\mathcal{S}}(x_{n}), (2) where 𝕀 \mathbb{I} denotes the identity operator, and 𝒫 𝒮 \mathcal{P}_{\mathcal{S}} and 𝒫 ℬ \mathcal{P}_{\mathcal{B}} represent the orthogonal projection operators onto 𝒮 \mathcal{S} and ℬ \mathcal{B} (see Appendix D.2 for details). However, excessive semantic alignment may inadvertently remove stylistic information. (4) The recomposed negation-aware embedding x ^ n \hat{x}_{n} is then injected into the frozen diffusion model, enabling negation-aware image generation while preserving the original semantic structure and visual style. 3.3 Theoretical Analysis In this section, we theoretically analyze the underlying mechanisms of Uni-directional SVD (Uni-SVD) and Bidirectional SVD (Bi-SVD), confirming how DeRO resolves the fundamental trade-off between bias suppression and style preservation. The proposed method not only suppresses undesirable biased semantics but also actively guides the representation toward the desired semantic direction while preserving the original semantic context and visual style of the input prompt. However, the proposed method still has limitations. Since semantic subspaces are estimated using auxiliary prompts, performance remains sensitive to prompt quality. Extending the method to more complex linguistic phenomena, such as relational and logical reasoning, remains an important direction for future work.
